whyThisMatters: Real security decisions are quick and the wrong option often sounds reasonable. Several bubbles here are habits people genuinely defend, such as one strong password everywhere or approving a prompt to make it stop. This game trains the reflex to judge the habit, not the label.
rememberThis: Sounding secure is not the same as being secure. Ask three quick questions: Is it unique per account? Did I start this request myself? Am I verifying through a channel the sender does not control? If any answer is no, slow down.

discussionPrompts: Ask which bubble people almost tapped wrongly. 'Reuse one strong password everywhere' is a favourite: one breach elsewhere lets attackers replay that password on other sites (credential stuffing).

Ask why approving an MFA prompt you did not start is bad even though MFA is good. The attacker already has the password and is hoping for fatigue; an unexpected prompt means the password is compromised and should be reported and changed.
Ask why SMS codes still count as good while a short password with symbols does not. Which attack does each stop, and which does it not?
Ask why 'Click Unsubscribe' in unknown spam is risky. It confirms your address is live and the link can lead to a tracking or fake page.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like security, or avoiding anything that sounds like a hassle, without asking what the habit really protects against. The 6 trick bubbles plus borderline habits such as Unsubscribe in spam, MFA prompts and cafe Wi-Fi banking catch that reflex.

bubbles.text: Turn on MFA for email and banking
Check the full sender address
Forward phish to security as attachment
Keep an offline, tested backup
Install updates within days of release
Password manager, unique passwords
Lock your screen every time you leave
Use company VPN on cafe Wi-Fi
Call back on a number you already have
Hover to see a link's real address
Phone-verify any bank detail change
Reuse one strong password everywhere
Click Unsubscribe in unknown spam
Approve an MFA prompt you did not start
Pause antivirus to run a tool faster
Share your login so a colleague can cover
Postpone updates for months
Cafe Wi-Fi, then banking without VPN
Use a free cracked licence key
Leave laptop unlocked for a quick coffee
Enable macros to view an invoice
Delay MFA setup because it is a hassle
SMS Code Received
bubbles.note: This is still a real second check after your password (MFA — Multi-Factor Authentication). A text code is weaker than an app code because attackers can sometimes redirect your phone number to their own device and read the code. But it is far better than only a password. "Better than nothing" is a real upgrade, especially where signal is limited.

bubbles.text: Long Passphrase (No Symbols)
bubbles.note: A long random phrase without symbols can still be stronger than a short "complex" password. Length matters more than adding symbols — a 16-character phrase beats an 8-character puzzle.

bubbles.text: Short Password + Symbols
bubbles.note: Symbols do not save a short password. Length matters more than looking complex. An 8-character password can be guessed quickly, no matter how clever it looks.

bubbles.text: Public Charging Cable
bubbles.note: A public USB port or cable at an airport or hotel can do more than charge — it can push harmful software or copy data through the same link that charges your phone. Use your own charger.

bubbles.text: Urgent Request From Senior Leader
bubbles.note: A senior title plus urgency is the classic trick. "The boss said..." or "The director needs this now..." is not proof a request is real. It is designed to make you skip your normal checks — such as calling back on a number you already trust.

bubbles.text: Old, Unpatched Virus Protection
bubbles.note: Virus protection (antivirus) that was installed last year and never updated does not help much against new threats. "Installed" is not the same as "up to date" — updates are what catch new harmful software.
